DILG Republic of the Philippines DEPARTMENT OF THE INTERIOR AND LOCAL GOVERNMENT DILG-NAPOLCOM Center, EDSA cor. Quezon Avenue, West Triangle, Quezon City www.dilg.gov.ph DILG OPINION No. 09 s. 2022 JAN 24, 2022 HON. ANDRES C. MONDARES Punong Barangay Barangay Cadulan, Municipality of Dimasalang, Province of Masbate Dear PB Mondares: This has reference to your letter dated 09 June 2021 wherein you are requesting for assistance in relation to the relocation of your Barangay Site and other barangay facilities. Per your letter, you stated the following facts: I. Empark Land Development Corporation has a proposed tourism project in the Municipality of Dimasalang that would entail acquiring land I properties wherein one of the affected barangays is Barangay Cadulan. Some barangay facilities and the entire barangay site of the said barangay would be affected by such development; 2. Empark Land Development Corporation have already identified a relocation site for the barangay facilities and families affected and also commit to defray the cost of the relocation and construction of the new barangay site and other infrastructures; 3. Located in the barangay site are Barangay Evacuation Center, barangay Health Station and community garden. Several houses are also constructed within the barangay site; 4. The land wherein the Barangay Hall, Multipurpose Hall and Plaza/Covered Court are situated in a private land where the proof of its donation to the barangay is yet to be verified and confirmed. 5. The Sangguniang Bayan of Dimsalang passed an Ordinance reclassifying the land of Barangay Cadulan in the Municipality of Dimasalang, Masbate to residential, commercial, industrial and tourism classifications. To begin with, among the numerous corporate powers that are granted to a barangay is the power to acquire and convey real and personal property, to wit: SECTION 22. Corporate Powers. — (a) Every local govemment unit, as a corporation, shall have the following powers: "Matino, Mahusay at Maaasahan" Trunkline No.: 8876-34-54

(1) xxx; (2) xxx; (3) xxx; (4) To acquire and convey real or personal property: xx xxx xxx (d) Local govemment units shall enioy full autonomy in the exercise of their proprietary functions and in the management of their economic enterprises, subject to the limitations provided in this Code and other applicable laws. Relatedly, we would like to invite your attention to the case of Sangguniang Panlalawigan of Bataan v. Congressman Enrique T. Garcia Jr. et al. (G.R. No. 174964, October 05, 2016), wherein the Supreme Court made a pronouncement regarding two established norms to determine the classification of the properties. According to the High Court, citing the case of The Province of Zamboanga del Norte v. City of Zamboanga, et al. (GR No. L-24440, Mar. 28, 1968), properties for the free and indiscriminate use of everyone are classified under the Civil Code as property for public use, while all other properties are patrimonial in nature. In contrast, under the Municipal Corporations Law, to be considered public property, it is enough that a property is held and devoted to a govemmental purpose, such as local administration, public education, and public health. It is therefore essential to distinguish between property for public use and patrimonial property for the reason that property of the provinces, cities, and municipalities for public use are outside the commerce of man, and cannot be leased, donated, sold, or be the object of any contract, except insofar as they may be the subject of repairs or improvements and other incidental things of similar character. On the other hand, patrimonial property is property owned by the state in its private or proprietary capacity which may be an object of ordinary contract. In administering the patrimonial property of municipalities, the municipal council occupies, for most purposes, the position of a board of directors of a private corporation. (Mendoza v. De Leon, G.R. No. L-9596, February 11, 1916) Correspondingly, as to the Ordinance reclassifying the land of Barangay Cadulan in the Municipality of Dimasalang, Masbate to residential, commercial, industrial and -tourism classifications, we would like to stress that mere reclassification of an agricultural land does not ipso facto allow the landowner thereof to change its use. Such reclassified agricultural lands must apply for conversion before the Department of Agriculture (DAR) in order to use the same for the said purpose. The Supreme Court, in the case of Chamber of Real Estate and Builders Associations, Inc. (CREBA) v. the Secretary of Agrarian Reform (G.R. No. 183409) explained: "Reclassification alone will not suffice to use the aqricultural lands for other purposes. Conversion is needed to change the current use of reclassified agricultural lands. It is of no moment whether the reclassification of agricultural lands to residential, commercial, industrial or other non-agricultural uses was done by the LGUs or by way of Presidential Proclamations because either way they must still undergo conversion process. It bears stressing that the act of reclassifying agricultural lands to non- agricultural uses simply specifies how agricultural lands shall be utilized for non-agricultural uses and does not automatically convert agricultural lands to non-agricultural uses or for other purposes. As explained in DAR Memorandum Circular No. 7, Series of 1994, cited in the 2009 case of Roxas & Company, Inc. v. DAMBA-NFSW and the Page 2 of 3

06 e6ed Department of Agrarian Reform,47 reclassification of lands denotes their allocation into some specific use and providing for the manner of their utilization and disposition or the act of specifying how agricultural lands shall be utilized for non-agricultural uses such as residential, industrial, or commercial, as embodied in the land use plan. For reclassified agricultural lands, therefore, to be used for the purpose to which they are intended there is still a need to change the current use thereof through the process of conversion. The authority to do so is vested in the DAR, which is mandated to preserve and maintain agricultural lands with increased productivity. Thus, notwithstanding the reclassification of agricultural lands to non-agricultural uses, they must still undergo conversion before they can be used for other purposes. " In view of the foregoing, the barangay facilities are of public dominion as it is devoted for public service. Note however that the actual barangay facilities are entirely different from the lot/site wherein it is situated. Hence, following the principles proclaimed by the Supreme Court in The Province of Zamboanga del Norte v. City of Zamboanga case, if the Civil Code will be applied, this Department opines that the lot is of patrimonial property since it is not available to the public compared to the actual barangay facilities. Also, in applying the Municipal Corporation Law, this Department is still of the considered view that the lot is patrimonial property since it is not entirely held and devoted to a governmental purpose, as several houses were also constructed therein. However, as to the Barangay Hall, Multipurpose Hall and Plaza/Covered Court, considering that the donation of the private land to the barangay, wherein these buildings are situated, is still yet to be verified and confirmed, we deem it proper to highlight that the property remains to be a private property as there is no such thing as an automatic cessation to government of lands, and that an actual transfer must be effected by the owner Be that as it may, this opinion is being rendered without prejudice to the opinion of more competent authorities. Thank you. Very truly yours, BY AUTHO OF THE SECRETARY RTIN . DINO Un ersecretary for Barangay Affairs COPY FURNISHED: DIRECTOR ANTHONY C.
